title: Assessment of Tropical Cyclones Over the Australian Region From Downscaled CORDEX‐CMIP6 Simulations
abstract: Tropical cyclones (TCs) cause major economic losses in Australia due to severe winds and floods; however global climate models (GCMs) are too coarse to properly resolve them. Here, we dynamically downscale ERA5 reanalysis and 16 CMIP6 simulations from 11 GCMs using the Conformal Cubic Atmospheric Model (CCAM) to a ∼10 km resolution over the Australian region. We evaluate whether these simulations can represent TC activity over the Australian region by analyzing TC frequency, genesis, intensity, lifespan, and the role of ocean–atmosphere coupling. The downscaled simulations reproduce observed spatial and seasonal patterns of TC activity, with the highest skill in the central and eastern subregions. CCAM‐ERA5 captures the observed intensity distribution for Categories 2–4 and the relationship between lifespan and intensity. The CCAM‐CMIP6 ensemble reproduces mean TC number well in the central and eastern subregions but underestimates the most intense (Categories 4–5) and medium‐lived TCs (6–8 days) while overestimating Category 1 systems. Ocean coupling has model‐dependent effects rather than producing a systematic improvement. Coupled configurations generally simulate fewer TCs than atmosphere‐only configurations, mainly through reduced weak‐TC numbers, while differences in stronger‐TC intensity are generally small and metric dependent. Overall, the CCAM downscaled simulations provide a realistic representation of Australian TC climatology, particularly in the central and eastern subregions, but remaining biases in the western basin and in the upper tail of TC intensity should be considered in future projection and impact applications.

title: Urban design interventions reduce fear of crime in public spaces in gender-sensitive ways
abstract:
Crime is a continuing urban challenge. This study, based in Chile, finds that design interventions are effective but less so as new ones are added and that interventions are more effective at reducing the fear of crime in men than women. 
 Fear of crime in public spaces is a major policy problem worldwide. Environmental Crime Prevention proposes that modifying the built environment can reduce the fear of crime, but key questions remain: are these interventions equally effective across genders, and what intensity maximizes safety perceptions while optimizing costs? Here we evaluated three interventions: ‘Eyes on the Street’ (adding windows to blind walls), neutral stimuli (removing graffiti by repainting walls) and ‘Nature-Based Solutions’ (integrating tidy vegetation into urban infrastructure) in the context of ‘Broken Windows’ disorder. Interventions were applied at varying intensities across four types of public spaces. Using a randomized experiment in Chile with photo simulations and an adapted Positive and Negative Affective Schedule, we collected 18,150 perception ratings from 2,028 respondents. The results show that perceived safety improvements are positive but nonlinear, indicating diminishing returns beyond a certain intervention intensity. Critically, responses were highly gender specific: interventions were more effective for men, suggesting that environmental changes alone do not fully address women’s perceived insecurity. Crime is a continuing urban challenge. This study, based in Chile, finds that design interventions are effective but less so as new ones are added and that interventions are more effective at reducing the fear of crime in men than women.

title: Household solid fuel combustion-related PAH exposure in rural northern China: Associations of phenanthrene metabolites with DNA damage and systemic inflammation
abstract:
•1-OHNap distinguishes respiratory exposures to PAHs in different solid fuels. •OH-PHEs dominated urinary OH-PAHs and were linked to 8-OHdG and CRP. •Exploratory BKMR suggested isomer-specific OH-PHE-biomarker associations. •4-OHPhe was the sole PAH metabolite independently associated with VEGF. 
 The relevance of urinary hydroxylated polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (OH-PAHs) to oxidative-stress and inflammatory biomarkers remains unclear, particularly in rural populations exposed to household solid-fuel combustion. In this cross-sectional study, we investigated urinary OH-PAH profiles and their associations with biomarkers of oxidative DNA damage, systemic inflammation, and vascular repair among 77 rural residents in northern China during winter. The summed concentration of ten urinary OH-PAHs (ΣOH-PAHs) ranged from 0.0499 to 7.0414 μg g−1 UCr. Hydroxylated phenanthrene metabolites (OH-PHEs) accounted for the largest fraction (44%), indicating phenanthrene as a major contributor to the internal PAH metabolite burden. Among metabolite groups, ΣOH-PHEs showed the strongest positive associations with 8-hydroxy-2′-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) and C-reactive protein (CRP). These results suggest that OH-PHEs may serve as priority internal-exposure biomarkers associated with oxidative DNA damage and systemic inflammation. Exploratory Bayesian kernel machine regression further suggested isomer-specific association patterns: 1-hydroxyphenanthrene (1-OHPhe) showed the most prominent signal for 8-OHdG, whereas 2-OHPhe and 3-OHPhe were more closely associated with CRP. In a small subset with paired airborne PAH measurements, exploratory mediation analysis yielded positive indirect-effect estimates for OH-PHEs in the association between airborne phenanthrene and 8-OHdG. These findings highlight phenanthrene metabolites as important PAH internal-exposure indicators in rural solid-fuel settings and support source-targeted exposure reduction and health-risk prevention.

title: Long-term exposure to multiple air pollution and trajectory risk of cardio-renal-metabolic multimorbidity
abstract:
•Air pollution was associated with cardio-renal-metabolic disease progression. •Pathways involving kidney damage showed heightened vulnerability. •Low-grade inflammation partly accounted for air pollution associations. •Healthy lifestyle adherence mitigated air pollution–related hazards. 
 BackgroundEvidence on how long-term exposure to multiple air pollutants contributes to the onset and progression of cardio-renal-metabolic disease (CRMD), including cardiovascular disease (CVD), type 2 diabetes (T2D) and chronic kidney disease (CKD), remains limited. We aimed to clarify these associations and further explore the potential biological intermediary role of low-grade inflammation.Methods369,168 UK Biobank participants were included to evaluate associations of individual pollutants and their mixtures with CRMD onset and progression. Joint effects were assessed via quantile g-computation. An inflammation score (INFLA score) was constructed for mediation analyses, with multivariable models adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, and lifestyle factors.ResultsDuring a median 13.6 years of follow-up, 76,871 participants developed a first CRMD (FCRMD), of whom 12,851 subsequently progressed to cardio-renal-metabolic multimorbidity (CRMM). Compared with the lowest quartile, participants in the highest PM2.5 quartile exhibited higher hazards of FCRMD (HR: 1.09, 95% CI: 1.06-1.11) and CRMM (1.22, 1.15-1.29). In multi-state models, each quartile increase in pollutant mixtures was associated with HRs (95% CI) of 1.02 (1.01, 1.03) for baseline to FCRMD and 1.04 (1.01, 1.06) for FCRMD to CRMM, with PM2.5 exhibiting the largest positive relative weight. Disease-specific analyses revealed heightened vulnerability along pathways involving CKD. INFLA score accounted for the associations between PM2.5 and CRMD with subtle mediated proportion, driven primarily by C-reactive protein. Stratified analyses demonstrated stronger hazard elevations among individuals with unfavorable baseline lifestyle profiles.ConclusionsLong-term exposure to multiple air pollutants was associated with elevated hazards of CRMD onset and trajectory progression, particularly for pathways involving kidney damage. These longitudinal associations may be partially accounted for by systemic low-grade inflammation, with adherence to healthy lifestyles mitigating environmental vulnerability.

title: Morphology of submicrometer water-insoluble particles in a Greenland ice core during recent and early twentieth-century periods: estimation of deposition fluxes of combustion particles
abstract:
•Fine water-insoluble particles in a Greenland ice core were analyzed by TEM. •1910 and 2013 samples were selected based on BC concentration and model simulations. •Organic aggregates found in 1910 samples imply wood combustion contributions. •Mass deposition flux of combustion particles was estimated using TEM and BC results. •Results suggest past substantial emissions of combustion organics along with BC. 
 Historically, anthropogenic combustion activities have emitted black carbon (BC) and organic aerosols into the atmosphere, contributing to global pollution and to the Earth's radiative balance. Detailed analyses of ice-core archives are important for improving our understanding of past aerosol emissions and their implications for climate. For this study, using a nebulizer system combined with water dialysis in addition to BC measurements with a Single Particle Soot Photometer (SP2), we conducted observations of transmission electron microscopy (TEM) samples of sub micrometer water-insoluble (WI) particles in an ice core from Southeast Greenland. We analyzed samples of 1910, a period when BC concentrations were high, and of 2013, when the model indicated large biomass-burning effects in summer but anthropogenic effects in the other seasons. A large proportion of WI particles were carbonaceous, including aggregates and spheres, with morphological features typical of combustion particles. Their mass deposition flux values (Fx) were estimated from TEM analysis results and BC concentrations. For 70–1000 nm WI particles, the Fx values of BC and organic-rich particles were 0.05–0.8 mg m−2 season−1 and 0.3–0.8 mg m−2 season−1 for 2013, and 0.5–1.7 mg m−2 season−1 and 0.5–1.2 mg m−2 season−1 for 1910. The Fx values of carbonaceous aggregates were higher in 1910 than in 2013, except in summer. Aggregates comprising mainly organics, which were almost absent from 2013 samples, were found in 1910 samples, along with soot-containing aggregates, implying contributions from wood combustion. These results suggest that anthropogenic combustion activities during the pollution period approximately 100 years ago emitted substantial amounts of submicrometer WI organic particles into the atmosphere along with BC. The combination of BC measurement and TEM analysis is expected to be useful for estimating the amounts of morphologically and compositionally categorized organic and trace metals when applied to various clean accumulated samples.
